subtopic_detail: Bedwetting most nights in a seven year old who is dry by day and has never had a dry spell lasting six months
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a seven year old boy whose parents want help with bedwetting. He wets five or six nights a week and has never been reliably dry overnight for longer than a fortnight. He is dry during the day, does not rush to the toilet, passes urine four to five times a day and opens his bowels daily without straining.

He has started avoiding school camps and a friend's sleepover, which is what prompted the visit. His parents have already tried lifting him at eleven each night and restricting drinks after dinner without benefit. There is no snoring and no daytime somnolence.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with no palpable bladder or faecal loading, normal external genitalia, normal lower limb tone power and reflexes, no sacral dimple or hair tuft, spine straight, growth along the fiftieth centile
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative for glucose protein leucocytes and nitrites, bladder diary shows age appropriate voided volumes with no urgency episodes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Prescribe oral oxybutynin at night and titrate the dose upwards over four weeks according to the response
options.rationale: Antimuscarinic therapy targets detrusor overactivity, which announces itself through daytime urgency, frequency and holding manoeuvres, none of which are present here. Using it for monosymptomatic bedwetting treats a mechanism this child does not have. (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis)

options.text: Continue nightly lifting and fluid restriction after dinner, and reassure the family that this resolves with age
options.rationale: Spontaneous resolution does occur at around fifteen per cent per year, but this family has already trialled these measures without effect and the child is now declining social activities. Lifting also trains a child to void while asleep rather than to wake to a full bladder. (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis)

options.text: Arrange a bedwetting alarm with structured family support and review the response after four to six weeks
options.rationale: An alarm is first line for monosymptomatic bedwetting in a child of this age, has the highest sustained success once treatment stops, and works by conditioning waking to the sensation of a full bladder. Success depends on the child waking fully and completing the routine, so structured support and a defined review point are part of the prescription. (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis)

options.text: Prescribe oral desmopressin nightly as an ongoing treatment and continue it until he becomes reliably dry
options.rationale: Desmopressin works quickly but relapse on withdrawal is common, which is why it is best used for short term cover such as a camp or sleepover rather than as the primary long term strategy. It also requires evening fluid restriction to avoid hyponatraemia. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for renal tract ultrasound and urodynamic studies before committing the family to any specific treatment
options.rationale: Imaging and urodynamics are reserved for children with daytime symptoms, a history of urinary infection, abnormal voiding or neurological signs, all absent here. Investigating a normal examination with a normal bladder diary delays the treatment that works. (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis)

explanation.summary: Nocturnal enuresis is defined as involuntary wetting during sleep in a child of five years or older, and the first branch point is whether it is monosymptomatic, meaning no daytime urinary symptoms at all. Monosymptomatic enuresis reflects a mismatch between overnight urine production, bladder capacity and arousal from sleep, and is treated with an alarm or desmopressin. Non monosymptomatic enuresis, signalled by urgency, frequency, holding manoeuvres or daytime wetting, points to bladder dysfunction and needs that treated first. Constipation is the single commonest reversible contributor across both groups and is specifically sought at every assessment. Secondary enuresis, meaning recurrence after six months of dryness, widens the differential to include diabetes, urinary infection, and psychosocial stressors including abuse.
key_points: Monosymptomatic enuresis means no daytime urgency, frequency, holding or wetting on careful history
The alarm is first line and has the best sustained response after treatment stops
Desmopressin acts rapidly but relapses on withdrawal, so it suits short term cover such as camps
Constipation is the commonest reversible contributor and is asked about at every assessment
Imaging and urodynamics are reserved for daytime symptoms, infection, or neurological findings
explanation.pearls: Alarm treatment is continued until the child achieves fourteen consecutive dry nights, and stopping earlier is the commonest reason for relapse, so set that endpoint with the family when you write the prescription.

subtopic_detail: Sudden painful clustered erosions of uniform size on eczematous skin with fever after contact with a relative with a cold sore
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a two year old girl with longstanding eczema whose mother reports that a rash on her face and neck changed character over twenty four hours. The child is now miserable, refusing to let anyone touch her face, and has stopped drinking well.

Her eczema is usually controlled with a moderate potency topical steroid and daily emollient. Her grandmother, who minded her three days ago, had a blister on her lip at the time. She has had no new foods, no new topical products and no recent antibiotics.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 152 beats per minute, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Clustered shallow erosions of uniform size with scalloped borders over both cheeks chin and anterior neck, some with haemorrhagic crust, no honey coloured crusting, tender cervical lymphadenopathy, eyelids involved to the lash line with no corneal staining on fluorescein
data_table.Investigations: Viral swab of a deroofed lesion sent for nucleic acid amplification testing, bacterial swab sent, results pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase the topical corticosteroid to a potent preparation and add twice daily wet dressings to the affected skin
options.rationale: Escalating topical steroid is the correct response to an eczema flare but is the wrong response to this pattern, and unopposed potent steroid over these lesions can allow the infection to extend. The uniform punched out morphology is what separates the two situations. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema herpeticum)

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin for seven days and arrange general practitioner review in two days for the skin
options.rationale: Bacterial superinfection of eczema is common and produces honey coloured crusting and pustules rather than uniform monomorphic erosions, and it is absent on this description. Treating only the bacterial possibility leaves the driving process untreated for a further two days. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admit for intravenous aciclovir with ophthalmology review, continuing emollients and withholding potent topical steroid
options.rationale: Widespread monomorphic punched out erosions on eczematous skin in a febrile unwell toddler after cold sore contact is treated as disseminated herpes simplex, and involvement above the lash line with systemic upset and poor oral intake makes the intravenous route appropriate. Ophthalmology review is needed because periocular disease can progress to keratitis even with a currently clear fluorescein examination. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema herpeticum)

options.text: Apply topical aciclovir cream five times daily to the affected areas and review the child in the clinic tomorrow
options.rationale: Topical antiviral has negligible penetration across a large disrupted surface and no effect on viraemia, so it does not treat disseminated disease. It is intended for a localised recurrent cold sore on intact skin in an otherwise well person. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Withhold all treatment until the viral swab result returns, providing analgesia and oral rehydration in the interim
options.rationale: Nucleic acid testing may take a day or more, and the recognised complications of untreated dissemination include keratitis, encephalitis and bacterial sepsis from the denuded surface. Treatment starts on the clinical pattern and is stopped later if the swab excludes the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema herpeticum)

explanation.summary: Eczema herpeticum is disseminated herpes simplex infection of skin whose barrier is already broken by atopic dermatitis, and it is a paediatric emergency because it can progress to keratitis, encephalitis and secondary bacterial sepsis. The discriminating morphology is monomorphic, meaning every lesion is a punched out erosion of roughly the same size and stage, which contrasts with the polymorphic pustules and honey crust of bacterial impetiginisation and with the ordinary excoriated plaques of a flare. Fever, pain out of proportion to the visible rash and a rapidly extending rash in a child with known eczema should all raise it. Contact with an active cold sore is supportive but often absent, since shedding occurs without visible lesions. Periocular disease requires ophthalmology review because herpetic keratitis threatens sight and may not be apparent on an initial examination.
key_points: Monomorphic punched out erosions of uniform size distinguish this from polymorphic bacterial impetiginisation
It is a paediatric emergency owing to risks of keratitis, encephalitis and secondary bacterial sepsis
Systemic aciclovir is the treatment, with the intravenous route for systemic upset or extensive disease
Potent topical corticosteroid is withheld over infected areas while emollients are continued
Periocular involvement mandates ophthalmology review even when fluorescein examination is initially clear
explanation.pearls: Pain is the symptom that separates eczema herpeticum from an ordinary flare: atopic dermatitis itches, while herpetic erosions hurt, so a child who resists any touch to previously itchy skin has changed diagnosis until proven otherwise.

subtopic_detail: Timing of a live attenuated vaccine after completing two months of high dose prednisolone for nephrotic syndrome
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a nephrology clinic reviewing a three year old boy who has just completed an eight week course of prednisolone at 2 mg/kg daily for his first episode of nephrotic syndrome. He is now in remission and off all treatment as of four days ago.

His mother asks about his overdue measles mumps and rubella and varicella vaccinations, which were deferred when he became unwell. His two year old sister is fully immunised and there are no household contacts who are immunosuppressed or pregnant. He has had no blood product or immunoglobulin exposure.

data_table.Examination: Weight tracking on the fiftieth centile, no periorbital or peripheral oedema, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, chest clear, abdomen soft with no ascites
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein creatinine ratio within normal limits, serum albumin 38 g/L (35-50), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about these two vaccines?

options.text: Give both vaccines today, since he is in remission and has been off corticosteroid therapy for several days
options.rationale: Immune reconstitution lags behind the clinical remission and the last dose by weeks, so vaccinating on the day treatment stops risks disseminated vaccine strain infection. Being off treatment is necessary but not on its own sufficient. (Source: NCIRS: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Give the measles mumps and rubella vaccine today and defer the varicella vaccine for a further twelve months
options.rationale: Both are live attenuated vaccines and share the same deferral rule after significant immunosuppression, so separating them in this way has no basis. Splitting them also leaves the child unprotected against the pathogen that causes more severe disease in this setting. (Source: NCIRS: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Withhold both vaccines permanently and rely on maintaining household and childcare contact immunity instead
options.rationale: Permanent contraindication applies to ongoing significant immunosuppression, not to a completed course in a child now in remission. Cocooning contacts is a useful adjunct but is not a substitute for direct protection in a child who can safely be vaccinated later. (Source: NCIRS: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Defer both live vaccines until at least one month after the last corticosteroid dose, then give them together
options.rationale: Prednisolone at 2 mg/kg daily for fourteen days or longer counts as significant immunosuppression, and live vaccines are deferred for at least one month after that course finishes to allow immune recovery. Both may then be given at the same visit, and if not given together they are separated by four weeks. (Source: NCIRS: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Check measles and varicella serology first and vaccinate only if the antibody titres return below protective levels
options.rationale: Serology is not used to decide whether to give routine childhood live vaccines in an unvaccinated child, since absent prior exposure makes a negative result the expected finding. It adds a blood test and a delay without changing the plan. (Source: NCIRS: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: Live attenuated vaccines replicate in the recipient, so significant immunosuppression converts an intended mild exposure into a risk of disseminated vaccine strain disease. Australian practice defines significant corticosteroid immunosuppression as prednisolone equivalent at or above 2 mg/kg daily, or 20 mg daily in a child over ten kilograms, continued for fourteen days or more. After such a course, live vaccines are deferred for at least one month once treatment has stopped. Lower doses, alternate day regimens, inhaled or topical corticosteroid, and physiological replacement do not require deferral at all. Inactivated vaccines can be given at any time, although the response may be blunted during treatment, which is a reason to time them thoughtfully rather than to withhold them.
key_points: Significant immunosuppression is prednisolone at or above 2 mg/kg daily for fourteen days or longer
Live vaccines are deferred at least one month after that course stops, not from the date of remission
Measles mumps rubella and varicella follow the same deferral rule and may be given at the same visit
Inhaled, topical, alternate day and replacement dose corticosteroids do not require any deferral
Inactivated vaccines may be given during immunosuppression, though the response may be reduced
explanation.pearls: Two live vaccines not given on the same day must be separated by at least four weeks, because the interferon response to the first blunts the take of the second and can leave the child inadequately protected.

subtopic_detail: Disc battery seen below the diaphragm on radiograph in an asymptomatic four year old who swallowed it two hours earlier
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a four year old girl who was found with an opened remote control two hours ago, and her father is certain that the twenty millimetre disc battery it contained is missing. She has had no drooling, no vomiting, no chest or abdominal pain, and she drank a cup of juice in the waiting room without difficulty.

She has no previous gastrointestinal surgery and no known swallowing problem. A single radiograph of the neck chest and abdomen has been performed.

data_table.Examination: Handling the situation calmly, no drooling, chest clear with no stridor, abdomen soft and non tender with normal bowel sounds
data_table.Investigations: Radiograph shows a twenty millimetre disc shaped radio opaque foreign body with a double ring halo sign lying in the gastric antrum, with no free gas beneath either hemidiaphragm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange emergency endoscopic removal within two hours regardless of the position shown on the radiograph
options.rationale: The two hour rule applies to a battery lodged in the oesophagus, where mucosal contact generates a hydroxide burn that can perforate within hours. Once the battery has passed into the stomach that contact is lost and the urgency changes entirely. (Source: RCH CPG: Button battery ingestion)

options.text: Give a dose of oral honey now and discharge her with advice to return only if she develops abdominal pain
options.rationale: Honey is given in the prehospital and pre removal window for a suspected oesophageal battery, where it coats the mucosa and buffers hydroxide generation, and it has no role once the battery is gastric. Discharging without a planned radiograph also removes the safety net that confirms passage. (Source: RCH CPG: Button battery ingestion)

options.text: Admit for observation with four hourly abdominal examination and a repeat radiograph before any discharge home
options.rationale: An asymptomatic child with a gastric battery and a normal abdomen does not need inpatient observation, and admission consumes a bed without altering the outcome. Written return advice covers the small risk of later symptoms just as effectively. (Source: RCH CPG: Button battery ingestion)

options.text: Discharge with written return advice and arrange a repeat radiograph in ten to fourteen days to confirm passage
options.rationale: A battery that has reached the stomach in an asymptomatic child of this age passes spontaneously in the great majority of cases, so observation at home with a defined imaging endpoint is appropriate. The repeat film identifies the minority that fail to progress and therefore need endoscopic retrieval. (Source: RCH CPG: Button battery ingestion)

options.text: Prescribe a stimulant laxative and a high fibre diet to accelerate transit, with review by the local doctor next week
options.rationale: There is no evidence that promoting transit changes the outcome for a gastric battery, and a laxative adds cramping that may confuse later assessment of abdominal pain. The decision point is whether the battery moves, not how quickly. (Source: Poisons Information Centre Australia)

explanation.summary: Disc battery ingestion is dangerous because current flowing at the negative pole hydrolyses tissue fluid and generates hydroxide, producing a liquefactive burn rather than a pressure injury, and this begins within two hours of mucosal contact. The whole management algorithm therefore turns on location. A battery in the oesophagus is removed emergently, ideally within two hours, and honey may be given before removal in a child over twelve months who can swallow and has no perforation signs. A battery that has passed into the stomach in an asymptomatic child is managed expectantly with a repeat radiograph, usually at ten to fourteen days, because spontaneous passage is the rule. Batteries twenty millimetres or larger, children under five years, and any symptomatic child prompt a lower threshold for earlier imaging and for endoscopic retrieval.
key_points: The injury is a hydroxide burn from current at the negative pole, beginning within two hours of contact
An oesophageal battery is removed emergently, ideally within two hours of ingestion
The double ring or halo sign on a plain film distinguishes a disc battery from a swallowed coin
A gastric battery in an asymptomatic child is observed with a repeat radiograph at ten to fourteen days
Failure to progress, or any new symptom, converts expectant management into endoscopic retrieval
explanation.pearls: Delayed catastrophic bleeding from an aorto oesophageal fistula can occur up to four weeks after an oesophageal battery has been removed, so any haematemesis in that window is treated as a surgical emergency rather than as incidental.
